20. In 1986, a report was issued by a Post task force which focused on recruitment, hiring, retention and advancement of blacks in the Post's newsroom, and which surveyed newsroom employees. Page 7 of that report stated "[t]hroughout the newsroom, sexism is seen as more prevalent than racism." See Declaration of Rick Ehrmann at Tab D.

21. In early 1987, I returned to work as a reporter covering the airline industry. According to my pay records at the Post, my salary was reduced about $47 per week at the same time--even though I understand that the practice is not to reduce editors' salaries when they return to working as reporters. Because pay records are not available to me, I do not know whether the men who moved from editor to reporter positions received a reduction in pay.

22. I covered the airline industry from 1987 until 1993. I covered the aftermath of airline deregulation, including the emergence of new carriers such as Presidential Airlines and the Pan Am Shuttle; the decline in airline service and on-time performance; the bankruptcies of major carriers such as Continental Airlines, Eastern Air Lines, and Pan American World Airways and the role of corporate airline executives including American Airlines Robert Crandall, Donald Trump and Frank Lorenzo. I was frequently on the front page. For instance, in 1989 I had 18 front page stories. And I regularly beat the competition, often covering -- either by myself or with Frank Swoboda (who had returned after his stint as AME) -- the same stories that the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times covered with a larger number of reporters. During this period, I produced frequent consumer service stories, including explainers on the airlines' increasingly sophisticated pricing of each airline seat and the hazards of overhead storage in aircraft cabins.

IN THE MATTER OF MARTHA HAMILTON,
CAROLINE MAYER, CYNTHIA L. SKRZYCKI,
SHARON W. WALSH AND THE WASHINGTON POST

Declaration of Martha McNeil Hamilton

I, Martha McNeil Hamilton, declare as follows:

1. My work experience prior to coming to the Post¹ included the following:

Reporter, The Newark News, 1966

Reporter, Freelance and stringer for Copley News Service, North American Newspaper Alliance and Time Magazine from Buenos Aires, 1966-67 which included, among other things, doing a series for Copley on the Antarctic

Writer and Assistant Editor, The Machinist, weekly, 1968

Reporter covering agriculture, oil and the Supreme Court, The New York Journal of Commerce, 1969-70

Assistant to the Dean and Acting Director of Admission, LBJ School of Public Affairs, University of Texas

Assistant Director, Agribusiness Accountability Project (public advocacy and research organization). In this job I also wrote articles for The New Republic and the Texas Observer

Author, The Great American Grain Robbery, published by the Agribusiness Accountability Project in 1972

2. I had an application pending at the Post for many months but hadn't heard from the Post until I received a call on a Sunday (I would learn later that this was just after the women in the news room had filed a sex

1 I have a B.A. in history, with a minor in classics from the University of Texas.

industry, often working 6 or 7 days a week and staying on the story in bankruptcy court in New York regularly to 2 or 3 a.m., Peter Behr was AME and, in that roughly five year period, Behr only gave me one merit increase -- in Nov. 1990. During the same period, I have reason to believe a number of men got more merit increases.

23. While I was covering the airline industry, I also was covering oil and energy. In the late 1980's AME Behr took me off of the oil and energy beat. The reason was not related to my performance; instead, he said he had been asked to do so in order that Tom Lipippmann, who was returning to the National staff as a reporter, could cover the beat for National.

24. In late 1991, the Financial section sent me to the Canary Islands to cover the aftermath of the suicide by press lord Robert Maxwell. I was asked to bulldog the autopsy report, while my colleague Paul Farhi was sent to London where most of the news about the collapse of Maxwell's empire was breaking. I was able to beat the competition (the NYT) on what the autopsy report would conclude. Paul Fahri, a reporter with less experience than me, received, I believe, merit increases in 1991 and in 1992 while I did not. In that year I also covered the collapse of Pan American World Airways and wrote an enterprise front page story: a tie test that tested the ability of consumers to differentiate the "silk" ties sold on the street versus designer ties and which reported on the actual fabric content, which was not silk.

25. In 1993, David Ignatius became Financial AME. A number of the women reporters in the section, very upset about treatment of women under AME Behr, asked to meet with Ignatius and his Deputy Doug Feaver to discuss issues that were of great concern to the women reporters. The event that triggered the meeting was the movement of reporter David Hilzenrath from the Real Estate Section to cover economics on Capitol Hill without the job having been posted or any of the current staff having been asked if they were interested. documents.title: Newsroom survey responses on race and sex at The Washington Post (printed page, two columns)
documents.subject: Printed compilation of anonymous employee survey/comment responses identified by race, sex, desk/section and role (e.g., 'White male, Photo/News Art:', 'White female, Metro, Reporter:'), discussing affirmative action, training, racism and sexism at the Post
documents.date: unknown (context suggests 1980s, related to Post newsroom task force surveys)
documents.notes: A single printed (typeset, two-column) page, torn along the outer edges. Content clearly differs from the declaration pages around it, so recorded as separate document. Appears to be reproductions of newsroom employees' survey comments — possibly an exhibit or internal publication related to the 1986 task force report cited in DOC-001. Bottom-right text is cut off at the page fold.

pages.transcript:
[Two-column printed page; edges torn. Left column:]

White male, Photo/News Art:
In its affirmative action program The Post does not seem to go far enough in recruiting the best candidates possible for the minority positions open.
There seems to be a shoot-from-the-hip approach which in the long run does neither the paper nor the individual any good. The Company gets stuck with someone who is second-best (at best) and the individual has to suffer because of his inability to perform.
Whereas greater effort to find the right minority — even though it takes more time money and effort, will pay off better in the long run for everyone.
If the company is truly serious about seeking out and promoting blacks and women, I feel it can done successfully, but it will take more effort than has been seen — in some cases — in the past.

White male, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:
I would hate to try to draw conclusions from such a poll.

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Editor:
I believe that The Post would benefit by having a greater diversity of social backgrounds in its reporters. This is true for editors, too. Race and sex are clearly important because they shape our outlook, both social class, urban-rural, geographical background, types of education and life experience all seem to me to be equally important. It has apparently changed over the years already, but if there is a "bias" in a pin-stripe, button-down, Eastern humor, style and cynicism that seems to matter most — for men, women, blacks or whites.
The Post does not tolerate oddsballs [sic] of any type very well. It has 3 hard time keeping soft journalists who see the world from a different perspective than news. It tends to select people who are tough and uncomfortable with genuine human emotions. The Post is not a steaming caldron of creativity, with excellence cutting across types of people and interests. It seems best typified to me by a kind of hip bureaucratic type. In my view, this is the larger question facing the paper. Dealing with sex and race is more responding to pressure form organized interest groups than it is facing that question.

White male, Metro, Reporter:
This questionnaire doesn't address a major problem: training for black reporters and editors after they get here. There is machinery in the Guild contract to provide this training, but it has been totally ignored by the company, as, in fact, most of the contract has been. I'm not talking about lunch with Dave Broder. What young blacks need is for more senior people to sit down with them and say "this story moves too slowly" or "this story lacks such-and-such." Set up a buddy system where a senior person takes a black under his or her wing. And set up regular evaluations (another contract provision that is honored in the breach). None of these problems are new. Nor are any of the solutions. What it will take is consistent, committed, structured effort by management — not the usual lip service.

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Editor:
Racism is a subtle thing — in the question about 'What percent of editors are prejudiced,' [his answer was 10-25%] I was talking about attitudes that the people involved would probably deny are racist.
The most obvious thing about racism at The Post is the contrast between the makeup of the staff and the population we try to cover.

[Right column:]

White female, Metro, Reporter:
The Post needs to do more to help all its new employees, blacks included, find their way through the bureaucracy and learn what kinds of stories the paper is looking for. Not just training seminars but personal attention from editors.
In addition, The Post body needs more women and blacks at the upper levels in REAL jobs, not token appointments overseeing training of blacks and women.

White male, Metro, Reporter:
National looks like a meeting of the White Citizens Council — clerks to copy aides to copy desk to correspondents.

White male, News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Editor:
Re: Question 22 & B [effect of race on Post career, length of Post employment]: with my skills, a black or woman would have more opportunities than I have at The Post.

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Reporter:
When I came to The Post, I was astounded at how few blacks I saw in The Post newsroom. I am still astounded.

White female, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Editor:
A look at the makeup of Outlook will give you a clear picture of the status of blacks and women at the WP.

White male, Metro, Reporter:
I think The Post needs to be more aggressive and thorough in finding minority reporters. But more importantly, we need to do a better job of supervising and training minority and beginning reporters at all races after they are hired. Too often young reporters are allowed to sink or swim on their own without having editors who have the time to work with them individually on a regular basis. Assignment editors are often too busy getting the next day's paper out and do not have the time to work with young reporters and really develop them.
One suggestion would be to have regular training seminars with small groups of reporters in which senior reporters and editors can explain how to use public records, how to develop sources and other basic skills. In the rare cases in which this is done usually the speakers are reporters like Broder and Woodward who are well-known and interesting, but are not close to the kind of reporting problems beginning reporters encounter.
In addition, these training seminars should be held over a set period of time in which the same people work with each other and discuss every-day problems. One other area that needs more attention is that in addition to more black reporters we need a lot of work on other minorities, particularly Chicanos, Puerto Ricans and Asians.

White male, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Editor:
One question that needs to be addressed is not so much racism (this survey alone shows an effort to do something about that) but snobbery. To some (but not all) in higher positions, education at an Ivy League school is more important than experience. That is particularly true for experienced employees hired from outside The Post. It is a problem that such an employee can overcome and often does overcome. (An Ivy League education is only one example of the factors that come into play, but apparently an important one.)

The arbitrator shall then issue a written decision, with reasons, that shall be final and binding on the parties.
